title: How a four-stroke car engine works

parts.label: Crankcase
parts.brief: A sturdy, rounded metal box at the bottom of the engine, cast in dull silver-grey aluminium. It has cooling ribs along its sides, a row of hex bolts around its top edge where the cylinder sits, and a small drain plug underneath.

parts.label: Crankshaft
parts.brief: A shiny steel shaft running left to right through the crankcase, with a chunky offset arm (crank throw) and heavy half-moon counterweights in the middle. Polished round bearing journals at each end, steel-blue with a slight oily sheen.

parts.label: Cylinder
parts.brief: A tall, hollow metal tube block standing on the crankcase, dark grey cast iron with thin cooling fins stacked around the outside. The inner wall is a smooth, polished bore where the piston slides up and down.

parts.label: Connecting Rod
parts.brief: A slim steel rod shaped like a long bone, with a small round eye at the top for the piston pin and a bigger split round end at the bottom held by two bolts around the crankshaft. Brushed silver colour.

parts.label: Piston
parts.brief: A short, thick metal can that fits snugly in the cylinder, silver aluminium with a flat, slightly darkened top. Three thin grooves with dark piston rings wrap around its upper side, and a round pin hole goes through its middle.

parts.label: Cylinder Head
parts.brief: A flat, heavy metal lid that caps the top of the cylinder, grey aluminium with a ring of bolts along its edge. It has two round ports on its front and back sides and a threaded hole on top for the spark plug.

parts.label: Intake Valve
parts.brief: A small mushroom-shaped steel valve: a thin stem with a wide round disc at the bottom, sitting in the back half of the cylinder head. Silver with a bluish tint, with a little coil spring around its stem.

parts.label: Exhaust Valve
parts.brief: A small mushroom-shaped steel valve just like the intake valve, sitting in the front half of the cylinder head. Its disc is darker and slightly scorched brown from hot gases, with a coil spring around its stem.

parts.label: Spark Plug
parts.brief: A small upright plug screwed into the top of the cylinder head. It has a white ceramic body with ridges, a silver hex nut in the middle, a metal tip on top for the wire, and a tiny hooked electrode at the bottom where the spark jumps.

parts.label: Intake Pipe
parts.brief: A short, round black pipe joined to the back side of the cylinder head, with a flanged metal end and bolts where it attaches. This is where fresh air and fuel come in.

parts.label: Exhaust Pipe
parts.brief: A short, round metal pipe joined to the front side of the cylinder head, coloured rusty bronze and dark grey from heat. It has a bolted flange where it meets the head and a slight bend at its open end.

steps.say: This is a car engine, the heart that makes a car go. Inside, tiny explosions push metal parts around and around. It works in four steps, called strokes. Let's take it apart and see!
Meet the piston. It slides up and down inside the cylinder, like a syringe plunger. A connecting rod links it to the crankshaft, which turns the up-and-down push into spinning.
Stroke one is intake. The piston slides down, the intake valve opens, and air and fuel get sucked in, just like you breathe in through a straw.
Stroke two is compression. Both valves close and the piston moves up, squeezing the air and fuel into a tiny space, like squashing a spring tight.
Stroke three is power! The spark plug makes a tiny spark, the fuel burns in a quick bang, and the hot gas shoves the piston down hard. This push turns the crankshaft.
Stroke four is exhaust. The piston comes back up, the exhaust valve opens, and the used gas gets pushed out the exhaust pipe, like breathing out.
Now it all goes back together. Suck, squeeze, bang, blow, over and over, many times every second. The spinning crankshaft sends that power to the wheels!

recap: A four-stroke engine repeats suck, squeeze, bang, blow, and the piston's push spins the crankshaft that drives the car.
question: What do you think would happen if the spark plug stopped making sparks?
